statement: A maximum output level specification must state balanced or unbalanced operation, the distortion criterion, the frequency range and the guaranteed load impedance.
A load impedance of 2 kOhm or greater is preferred for line-level outputs; 600 Ohm operation is obsolete except for specialized broadcast and telecommunications applications.
A laser-trimmed differential amplifier such as the THAT 1246 or 1286 provides typically 90 dB common-mode rejection; the untrimmed 1256 or 1296 provides typically 50 dB.

A discrete-resistor difference amplifier's common-mode rejection is limited by resistor matching: 1% resistors give worst-case CMR as low as 31.5 dB, 0.1% gives 51.5 dB, and matching the laser-trimmed 1246/1286 requires at least 0.01%.

Line-input impedance is a tradeoff: lower impedance lowers the noise floor, while higher impedance preserves common-mode rejection when the differential sources have slightly different low output impedances.
A line-input attenuator with more attenuation provides more headroom; at -6 dB system gain a THAT 1512 line input accommodates +27.5 dBu, has -100 dBu input-referred noise and 127.5 dB dynamic range.
A balanced U-pad changes its attenuation when the source switches from balanced to unbalanced, while two L-pads maintain the same attenuation for either source type.
Two 10 dB gain stages provide about 20 dB, enough for a preamplifier stage while allowing for the losses of volume and balance controls.

Few power amplifiers need more than about +4 dBV (1.58 V RMS) input for full power; a preamplifier delivering 5-6 V RMS will drive any amplifier, which is easily achieved with +/-12 V supplies although +/-15 V is usually preferred.
The NE5534 is stable only at a gain of three or more unless an external compensation capacitor is added, and it can oscillate in a unity-gain circuit.
locator: Opamp Testing, paragraph before the measurement board description

statement: A passive James or Baxandall bass and treble control has about 20 dB insertion loss, so a gain of 10 is needed to restore the level with the controls set for nominally flat response.

An active Baxandall tone control requires an inverting amplifier stage with low output impedance to drive the filter network, and gives approximately symmetrical boost and cut; with the values shown the maximum is about +/-15 dB.

A guitar tone stack has no true flat setting, produces a midrange scoop, and has insertion loss of about 8 dB for a Marshall-style stack to about 15 dB for a Fender-style stack with the controls centred.
Simple RC tone-control circuits have a theoretical maximum slope of 6 dB/octave.

Tone-control circuits require a low or very low impedance source and a high impedance load; input buffers are essential even when the input uses an inverting op-amp stage, because insertion loss depends on source impedance.
locator: Note at the start of the circuit descriptions and Section 4

statement: A graphic equalizer can have a Q that varies with boost and cut, or a constant Q; the constant-Q design sums band-pass filter outputs and keeps the filter loading constant.
A three-band Baxandall tone control has a Q of about 0.5, so it cannot make a narrow midrange correction.
locator: Section 4, Baxandall Active Tone Control With Midrange

statement: A passive Baxandall or James tone control has a flat-response error of up to about +/-2 dB and interactive controls, so a true flat position is difficult to achieve.
For a tone-control network, doubling the capacitance halves the frequency; changing the capacitance by a factor of 1.5 changes the frequency by the same fraction.
locator: Section 4, paragraph on calculating component values

statement: In a guitar tone stack the midrange control only reduces the depth of the notch, the notch frequency varies with control settings, and the controls are interactive.
The Fender-style guitar tone stack has more bass and treble boost and a deeper notch than the Marshall-style stack; the notch varies from about 300 Hz to 1 kHz for both.
THAT Design Note 140 suggests a common-mode choke as part of the RFI network for a microphone preamplifier.
At low levels of no more than 1 V peak, an RC4580 op-amp can drive a 200 Ohm load without showing increased distortion.
ESP measured all audio-grade op-amps flat from DC to at least 100 kHz (+/-0.1 dB) in a 10 dB gain circuit.
The bass response of an op-amp circuit is determined by passive components, almost always capacitors; the op-amp itself has no effect on bass response.
A differential-to-single-ended converter removes the common-mode signal, while a balanced output can be made with cross-connected differential amplifiers.

When two microphone preamps are multed, only one preamp's phantom power should be on; type A switching halves the phantom voltage because of the off preamp's DC load, so types B and C are recommended for mults.
High-gain preamplifiers can rectify radio frequencies, causing audible interference.
RF bypass capacitors should be returned to the connector shield with the shortest possible path.
A maximum gain specification is measured with all level and gain controls at maximum, using a 1 kHz input that does not clip the output, and must state whether the output is balanced or unbalanced.
A missing power-supply bypass capacitor close to the op-amp can cause oscillation, and the oscillation may not be visible on the output when viewed with a scope.
locator: Opamp Testing, paragraph before the measurement board description
